claims.text: The initial refractory high-entropy alloy is single-phase and typically BCC.
The initial alloy contains no intentionally added carbon.
The intervention adds approximately 0.5 at% carbon, or a comparable minor amount.
A tailored post-synthesis heat treatment is used together with carbon addition.
Carbon addition and tailored heat treatment will form nanoscale carbide precipitates.
The resulting nanoscale carbide precipitates will be uniformly dispersed within the alloy matrix.
Fine carbide precipitates impede dislocation motion through pinning.
Impeded dislocation motion increases yield strength.
Fine carbide precipitates promote strain hardening by facilitating controlled dislocation accumulation.
The proposed strain-hardening response helps maintain or improve ductility.
The carbon-added, heat-treated alloy will have roughly 10–20% greater yield strength than the carbon-free baseline.
The carbon-added, heat-treated alloy will maintain or slightly enhance plasticity relative to the carbon-free baseline.
The predicted improvement requires the carbide dispersion to remain fine and uniform.
Excess carbon or suboptimal heat treatment may produce coarse carbides or phase segregation.
Coarse carbide formation or phase segregation may negate the beneficial effects and cause embrittlement.
The expected behavior applies under quasi-static tensile loading at or near room temperature.

contradictions.description: The predicted outcome says plasticity will be maintained or enhanced, but the falsification rule permits a ductility decrease of up to 10% without necessarily falsifying that prediction.

The boundary makes formation of fine, uniform carbides a precondition for the hypothesis to apply, whereas the falsification rule treats failure to form those carbides as falsification rather than failure to realize the stipulated intervention.
